correctness.rationale: For arbitrary n, B, symmetric W and gamma>=1, the max-row-sum proof gives rho<=wmax(B^2/4)^gamma. A strongest-edge, equal-area two-node block attains it. Perron left-vector equality on an irreducible block forces all participating areas to B/2 and thus exactly two nodes. The three-site counterexample has exact eigenvalues and exact comparison inequality. checker.py passed 8,103 finite diagnostics; those are not used as a universal proof.

originality.rationale: Accessible primary texts establish eigenvalue capacity and various restoration/fragmentation optimizations but do not state or imply the exact general fixed-affinity, area-elastic, maximum-edge two-site allocation and its sharp equality characterization. Actual research-record queries also returned related but structurally different aims. The comparison is provisional because several older full texts could not be inspected. The counterexample for weaker elasticity is an explicit new calculation in this precise kernel.
residual_risks: The full Hanski–Ovaskainen (2000), Etienne–Heesterbeek (2000), Etienne (2004) and Nicol–Possingham (2010) texts could not all be inspected; hidden propositions or appendices could cover the result.
The row-sum method is classical and could have been applied to the same specialized design objective in works not located by the searches.
The area-exponent kernel is a selected spectral surrogate, not a universal ecological process model.

value.rationale: A fully quantified global design rigidity result for every network size and every fixed symmetric dispersal landscape: maximizing the stated capacity proxy necessarily deletes all but one strongest link, a materially important modeling degeneracy for habitat allocation. A three-site counterexample proves that this collapse is sensitive to the area exponent. This exact classification identifies when a connectivity-only spectral objective is unsuitable as a literal conservation planner; it is not merely a numerical recomputation of a known table.
